`.pi` files as modules, with HMR, dependency tracking (through
`piton compile --dependencies`) and virtual modules. Each export in the Piton
file is a named export, and the default export is the whole file, the same as
`piton compile` gives:

```ts
import { SaveButton } from '../spec/app.pi';
import spec from '../spec/app.pi';

const button = SaveButton;
const cancel = spec.CancelButton;
```

It has a configurable default renderer (`renderer: 'json' | 'yaml' |
'markdown'`), and the renderers can also be imported as functions
(`vite-plugin-piton/renderers`) and used inline. `packages/astro-piton` is an
Astro integration that wraps the Vite plugin.

## 15. Working on a specbase

1. **Orient.** Open `piton.config.pi` to find `root`, `entry`, `output`, the
   frameworks, the adapters, `codeRoot` and `shapeRoot`. Read the entry file,
   usually `spec/index.pi`, because its exports are the compilation roots.
   Follow the `index.pi` files down through the modules. In this repository,
   `spec/index.pi` exports `Specification` (FoundingThesis, Language, Tooling,
   Belay, PackageManagement) plus the skills and command in `spec/agent/`.
2. **Read compiled reference for overview, and source for truth.**
   `<referenceRoot>/**/*.md` is easy to browse, and its links are lazy, so
   follow them only when relevant.
3. **Edit the `.pi` source**, following the conventions around it:
   - one exported anchor per file, named after the file;
   - `index.pi` files that re-export with `from ./X export *`;
   - abstract anchors exported with a keyword, and shared abstracts in a
     `lib/` folder;
   - lowerCamelCase property names;
   - SCREAMING_CASE for exported constant lists;
   - prose in string blocks, and structure in keys and lists;
   - `@{X}` to link related documents;
   - examples inside fences wrapped in a `\\\` escape block.
4. **Keep imports honest.** Use `use` for keywords and `from ... import` for
   names; a file often needs both. A new file only compiles if the entry
   reaches it, so export it through an index or reference it.
5. **Validate.**
   - Run `piton check`.
   - `piton check` does **not** compile the examples inside escape blocks
     (they are literal text). When you edit spec examples, extract each ` ```piton ` block,
     run `piton compile` on it, and compare with any ` ```json ` block that
     follows. Remember that compile output has only exported names.
   - Run `piton build`, then look at the diff of the generated files.
   - Run `piton reach` to confirm new anchors are reached.
   - Run `piton format --check`.
6. **Never hand-edit generated files.** That includes `CLAUDE.md` and
   `AGENTS.md` under `codeRoot`, everything under `.claude/`, `.codex/`,
   `.agents/`, `.opencode/` and the build output directory that is listed in
   `.piton/manifest.json`, and the files in `.piton/` themselves.
7. **Keep implementation and spec in agreement.** The implementation is judged
   against the spec. When they disagree, report it instead of quietly bending
   the spec to fit. Trust `piton compile` for how things behave today, and
   flag the gap.

## 16. Where the compiler differs from the spec

Checked with `piton compile` and `piton build`:

- The CLI has a few things the spec doesn't name: `build --dry-run`,
  `tether --as`, agent argument passthrough, the `reach` flags, and
  `format` with no path or `-`.

- **Paragraph breaks.** The spec says a blank line in a string block starts a
  new paragraph. The compiler joins the paragraphs with a single `\n`, which
  Markdown output renders as one paragraph with a soft line break.

surprise you:

- A `/`-rooted import inside an installed package resolves against the
  consuming project's root, not the package's. Use relative imports inside a
  package.
- A required property from an abstract is not satisfied by a value inherited
  from a concrete base (`needs Thing extends Base`, where `Base` supplies it):
  the keyword's anchor comes last, and its value-less declaration wins. Give
  the value on the anchor itself.

  nothing imports is not checked. Name it: `piton check path/to/file.pi`.

  is hardcoded in `crates/piton-belay/src/adapter.rs`, not declared in the

# Body Scope

## How To Build

A BodyScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A BodyScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

The main window's body: the area to the right of the project sidebar, where the tasks sent to the harness, and the files opened in tabs beside them, are shown, and the chat input they are sent from.

### Shape

#### Description

Beneath the [RibbonScope](../../ui/components/ribbon/index.md#ribbon-scope), to the right of the [ProjectSidebarScope](../../ui/components/project-sidebar/index.md#project-sidebar-scope), which runs the full height beside it, and reaching the window's right edge. It is part of the [PromptEditor](../prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor).
The [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) lives within the body, along its bottom: its left edge against the project sidebar, and above it, beneath the body's tab bar, the selected tab's contents: the message list, or an open file. While a task runs, the [RightSidebarScope](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar-scope) runs the body's full height at its right, beside the tab bar, the selected tab's contents, and the chat input, and the chat input's right edge is against it: the chat input never runs beneath the right sidebar. While that sidebar isn't there, the chat input reaches the window's right edge.
The body is flat and quiet: the selected tab's contents, the message list or an open file, sit on the theme's base surface, #444444 in dark mode, running edge to edge with no border, and the chat input along the bottom is set apart from them only by its own darker tab strip, as the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) says, with no line between them.

#### Sliding

Whenever something slides out or back along one of the body's edges, as the [RightSidebarScope](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar-scope) does, everything else in the body moves smoothly with it, frame by frame, rather than jumping once the slide is over: the tab bar, the selected tab's contents, and the chat input all keep their right edge against the sliding edge throughout, so they narrow or widen together, in step with it and with each other. None of them lags behind another, is left at its old width until the slide settles, or runs beneath what is sliding. Their contents are laid out anew at each width as it changes, text wrapping and rows reflowing as they go: the tab bar's tabs, the chat input's text and buttons, the message list's table, and an open file's editor. A slide that reverses partway moves them back from wherever it had reached.

#### Contents

Everything that can be in the body:

- a tab bar along its top, holding a Chat tab and a tab for each file open
- the [MessageList](../prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list), the chat history, shown beneath the tab bar while the Chat tab is selected
- the hint shown in the message list's place before any task has been sent, or while no project is open, as the [PromptEditor](../prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor) and the [NoProjectStateScope](../no-project/index.md#no-project-state-scope) say
- an [EditorScope](../editor/index.md#editor-scope) for each open file, shown beneath the tab bar while its tab is selected
- the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope), along the bottom beneath whichever tab is selected
- the [RightSidebarScope](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar-scope), at the right of all of these, the tab bar and the chat input included, while a task runs

An [InsetPanelScope](../../ui/components/inset-panel/index.md#inset-panel-scope) floats over the whole window, the body included, but is never part of it.

#### Tabs

Along the top of the body runs a tab bar, in gpui-kit's default tab styling, across the width the message list takes: from the project sidebar to the right sidebar while a task runs, and to the window's right edge otherwise. Its first tab, Chat, shows the message list, and is always there: it can't be closed or moved. After it comes a tab for each open file, in the order they were opened unless they have been dragged since, scrolling sideways once there are more than fit.
Just one tab's contents show at a time, filling the space between the tab bar and the chat input. The chat input stays along the bottom whichever tab is selected, so a prompt can be written while a file shows. The body starts with Chat selected, and clicking a tab selects it.
Every tab in the bar, Chat and each file's alike, is laid out the same plain way, with nothing extra around it: the bar's full height, 32 pixels, its contents centred up and down in it, 12 pixels of padding at its left, and 12 at its right, and no margin of its own above, below, or beside it, so one tab ends where the next begins, with only the tab styling's own line between them. Nothing is inset from the bar's top or bottom, and the first tab starts at the bar's left edge.
A file's tab shows the file's name, then, while it has unsaved changes, a dot, and then a small close button, an icon button 16 pixels square, set close beside the name, 4 pixels from it or from the dot, with no more room between them however long or short the name is. Since the button has room of its own around its icon, a file tab's right padding is 6 pixels rather than 12, so the icon sits as far from the tab's right edge as the name does from its left; the tab is only as wide as its padding, name, dot, and close button need. Chat's spinner, while something runs, sits 6 pixels after its label, inside the same padding. Hovering a file's tab shows the file's path in the project as its tooltip.
A file's tab can be dragged along the tab bar to reorder the files, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, a vertical line showing the gap between two tabs it will land in, and the tab dragged following the pointer as the file's name. Chat stays first: no gap before a file's first tab, between Chat and it, shows the indicator, and Chat itself can't be dragged. Dragging a tab selects it, as clicking it does, and the selection follows the tab to its new place; nothing else about its editor changes. A press on a tab's close button closes it rather than starting a drag. A file opened afterwards still gets its new tab just after the one selected.

#### Open File

A file opened, from the [FileTreeScope](../../ui/components/file-tree/index.md#file-tree-scope) or anywhere else the [OpenFileScope](../open-file/index.md#open-file-scope) says, shows in an [EditorScope](../editor/index.md#editor-scope) in a tab of its own, as many files open at once as are opened. A file not open yet gets a new tab, just after the one selected, and is selected. Opening a file that already has a tab selects that tab instead, leaving its editor as it was, unsaved changes and all.
Nothing slides: a file's tab is selected, and its editor shows, at once, and closing it takes it away at once too. There is no split, and no edge to drag; the file takes the tab bar's full width above the chat input.
Closing a file's tab, with its close button or the editor's, closes the file, the editor first asking to discard any unsaved changes. Closing the selected tab selects the tab to its right, or, with none to its right, the one to its left, which is Chat once no file is left. Closing a tab that isn't selected leaves the selection as it is.

use /lib
from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts import ModeSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from /scope/spec-build import SpecBuildScope

export scope PromptModesScope:
    concept: {PromptModesConcept}

concept PromptModesConcept:
    pitch:
        The modes a prompt is sent in, each for a different kind of work on the
        code and the spec.

    shape: {PromptModesShape}

shape PromptModesShape:
    description:
        There are five modes, and wherever they are listed, they are in this
        order.

    modes:
        - Code: changes the code, leaving the spec as it is; a subtle red
        - Chain: changes the code and the spec together; purple
        - Spec: changes the spec, leaving the code as it is; a subtle blue
        - Ask: asks a question about the code and the spec, changing neither; a subtle green
        - Freeform: passes the prompt to the agent just as it is written; grey, the theme's tertiary text colour

    colours:
        Whatever shows a mode, or something sent in it, takes the mode's
        colour, a tint of the @{ThemeScope}'s hue of that name, readable in
        both light and dark mode. Chain is Code and Spec
        together, so wherever it shows Code and Spec as well, both are purple:
        the colour midway between Code's and Spec's. A colour chosen for Code,
        Chain, Spec, or Ask in the theme editor, as the @{ThemeScope} says,
        is used in place of that mode's, Chain staying midway between Code and
        Spec unless it is chosen too.

    tasks:
        A prompt sent in Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform is a task, sent as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says. Tasks carry on one conversation, one at a
        time, and queue while the harness is working. Before one is sent, the
        spec is built ahead of it, as the @{SpecBuildScope} says. Once one
        finishes without error, having changed files, it adds a commit note to
        the @{GitPanelScope}.

    questions:
        A prompt sent in Ask is a question. It runs straight away, alongside
        any task and any other question, and never queues, builds the spec, or
        adds a commit note. Questions carry on a conversation of their own,
        apart from the tasks', as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says.

    freeform:
        A prompt sent in Freeform is passed to the harness exactly as it was
        typed, with anything attached to it, and nothing else: no system
        prompt, no hidden anchor compiled from it, no spec built ahead of it,
        no slices, whatever the Slice toggle says, and no understanding file.
        Otherwise it is a task like any other: it queues while the harness is
        working, carries on the tasks' conversation, heads the message list,
        is saved in the prompt history, can be cancelled or resent, and adds a
        commit note once it finishes having changed files. It is saved in the
        history as a hidden anchor like any task's, recording its mode, so the
        queue and history hold it as they hold the others, but that anchor is
        never compiled, imports nothing, and has no system prompt. Its header
        shows the prompt as it was sent, with no hidden anchor named, and the
        right sidebar doesn't slide out while it runs, since it
        references nothing. What is sent to a running Freeform task, from Send
        to task, goes just as it was typed too. It is never sent to another
        mode, alone or in a batch.

    systemPrompts:
        Each mode but Freeform sends its own system prompt, from the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope}. A prompt keeps the mode it was sent in while
        it waits in the queue.

from /scope/prompt-mode/message-list import MessageList

export ui-component AnswerDrawerScope:
    concept: {AnswerDrawerConcept}

concept AnswerDrawerConcept:
    pitch:
        A drawer over prompt mode for reading an answer, or looking back
        through previous ones, without losing sight of where they came from.

    shape: {AnswerDrawerShape}

shape AnswerDrawerShape:
    description:
        The drawer slides up over the @{MessageList} and any file beside it.
        Only two things are a drawer: a question open onto its task table, and
        the previous answers expanded. Unlike the stack of question rows, which
        pushes what is above it, the drawer covers what is above it rather than
        pushing it. Closing it slides nothing back; the stack and the message
        list are where they were beneath it.

    questionRows:
        The drawer never covers the question rows still in the stack, so a
        question still running stays in view, its row following the harness,
        whatever is open. Whether it is a question open onto its table or the
        previous answers, the drawer slides up from on top of the rows in the
        stack rather than out of the chat input over them, leaving those rows
        where they were, uncovered and undimmed, and its share of the space
        counts from the chat input, rows included. As rows come and go, the
        drawer's bottom follows the top of the stack. With no rows left in the
        stack, it slides up out of the chat input.

    height:
        The drawer opens to 80% of the height of the space above the chat input
        by default: the open question's table, or the previous answers list,
        grows to fill whatever the drawer's other rows leave, rather than
        stopping at a fixed height. It slides up as it opens, and slides back
        down as it closes, whatever closes it: a question's heading clicked,
        the previous answers collapsed, a question closed, or the Ask tab left.
        It slides down to where it slid up from, the top of the question rows
        in the stack, or the chat input when there are none, showing what it
        held until it is gone, while the shade fades out. Opening another
        question, or switching between a question and the previous answers,
        changes what the drawer holds rather than sliding it down and up
        again.

        While open, the drawer is resizable by dragging its top edge, which
        shows a resize cursor and a thin highlight when hovered. It follows the
        pointer exactly, with no slide, and can be dragged from 20% to 95% of
        that space. The size it is dragged to is kept for as long as the
        application runs, for every question or list opened afterwards, rather
        than going back to 80%.

    dimming:
        While the drawer is open, a dark shade fades in over what it covers, to
        draw attention to it, and fades back out when it closes. The shade
        covers all the space above the chat input beneath the drawer: the
        selected tab's contents, the message list or a file, but not the
        body's tab bar, nor the question rows
        the drawer sits on top of. Question rows in the
        stack, running or finished, never dim anything themselves; they push
        the message list up instead.

from /scope/prompt-mode/answer-drawer import AnswerDrawerScope

export shape MessageListAskDimmingShape:
    description:
        While the @{AnswerDrawerScope} is open, it dims the message list beneath
        it.

from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope
from /ui/components/task-table import TaskTableScope

export ui-component HistoryListScope:
    concept: {HistoryListConcept}

concept HistoryListConcept:
    pitch:
        A way back to everything sent before of one kind, such as previous tasks
        or previous answers: a small row that expands into a list of every one
        of them.

    shape: {HistoryListShape}

shape HistoryListShape:
    description:
        The same row and list, looking and behaving the same, wherever something
        sent before can be looked back on. Each use names what it lists, what
        the row counts, and what the row reads while expanded.

    row:
        A small row, always shown where it is used, with the tab bar's
        background colour. It reads "No …", "1 …", or "N …" followed by what it
        counts, beside a chevron, and does nothing until there is anything to
        list. Clicking it expands the list, and the row then reads what it says
        to go back; clicking it again closes the list.

    list:
        A scrollable accordion of every item, oldest first, with a
        @{ScrollbarScope}. Each time it is expanded, it opens scrolled to the
        bottom, with the most recent items in view, however it was scrolled when
        last closed, the first time as much as any other, and whether it takes
        the place of the latest task or slides up as a drawer. Each is headed by
        its status and the first line of its prompt, with a Resend button at
        its right, when the use offers one, and opens onto the compiled
        prompt it was sent as and its @{TaskTableScope}. One item is open at a
        time. A use can say its tables collapse the steps leading up to the
        result, as previous answers do; previous tasks show their tables whole.

        An open item is exactly as wide as the list, however long the lines
        in its prompt or table, which wrap rather than running past the
        list's edge, and exactly as tall as what it shows: it ends a small
        margin below its table, like the margin above its prompt, with no
        empty space beneath it before the next item or the end of the list.

        However long an open item's output, the list lays out only what is in
        view: an open item's prompt, its table's header, and each of its
        table's rows are drawn as the list scrolls to them, as each item's
        heading is.

use /lib
use /ui
from ./chat-input import ChatInputScope
from ./message-list import MessageList
from ./queue-list import QueueListScope

export ui-component PromptEditor:
    concept: {PromptEditorConcept}

concept PromptEditorConcept:
    pitch:
        An interface for sending tasks to a local coding harness like Claude
        Code, written directly with compiled-on-depand Piton.

    shape: {PromptEditorShape}

shape PromptEditorShape:
    description:
        Not a chat. Each prompt sent is a task for the harness, tasks can
        queue, and each task shows its output until it finishes. There are no
        message bubbles.

    basicDesignAndLayout:
        The @{MessageList} fills the body's Chat tab: all the space between
        the body's tab bar and the @{ChatInputScope} along the bottom. From top to bottom it holds the
        previous tasks row, the header for the latest task, the latest task's
        output, and the queue.

        Before any task has been sent, the space shows a hint instead, which
        wraps when the view is narrow. It reads
        "Write a prompt below. Enter adds a line; Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it."
        or, while no project is open, as the @{NoProjectStateScope} says,
        "Open a project to start prompting."

    chatHistory: @{MessageList}

    previousTasks:
        Previous tasks are a @{HistoryListScope} along the top of the view,
        listing every task sent. Its row counts every task but the latest,
        which heads the view: "No previous tasks", "1 previous task", or
        "N previous tasks", and each offers Resend. Expanded, the list takes the place of the latest
        task and its output, and the row reads "Back to the latest task".

        Every task in the list has a checkbox at the left of its heading,
        before its status, and clicking it selects or deselects the task
        without opening or closing it. Shift-clicking one selects every task
        between it and the one last clicked, never deselecting any; with none
        clicked before, it selects or deselects that one as a plain click
        does. The selection is kept while the list is closed and opened again,
        until it is cleared or sent. Each open project keeps its own, as the
        @{OpenProjectsScope} says. Previous answers have no checkboxes.

        While any task is selected, the row shows the batch actions at its
        right, in place of nothing: "N selected", muted, counting every task
        selected, then "Send N to Spec" and "Send N to Code", small ghost
        buttons with a swap icon, each tinted the colour of the mode it sends
        to, then "Clear", which deselects them all. Send N to Spec counts, and
        sends, the selected tasks that offer Send to Spec, and Send N to Code
        those that offer Send to Code, as the @{PromptSendingScope} says; each
        is shown only while its count isn't zero. Tasks that don't offer it,
        sent in Chain or Freeform, whose mode isn't known, already sent to the
        other mode or being sent there, marked done, or complete, can be
        selected, and are counted in "N selected", but neither action sends
        them. Clicking an action never opens or closes the list.

        A batch action sends each of its tasks to the other mode, as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says for one, oldest first: the first starts
        straight away while the harness is free and the rest queue behind it,
        so they run in the order they were first sent, each saved in the
        history as a new task. Once sent, the tasks it sent are deselected,
        the rest of the selection is kept, and the list stays as it was, still
        expanded, with nothing opened. With no project open, it sends nothing,
        a notification says a project must be opened first, and the selection
        is kept.

    previousTaskFilters:
        While the previous tasks are expanded, a filter bar sits along the top
        of the list, beneath their row and above the first item, on the tab
        bar's background with the theme's line beneath it, and scrolls with
        nothing: it stays put as the list scrolls. It holds two groups of
        small toggle chips, the second set 12 pixels apart from the first,
        wrapping onto another line when the bar is too narrow. Each chip
        reads its label and, muted after it, how many previous tasks match
        it on its own, whatever other chips are on; the latest task, heading
        the view, is never counted.

        The first group filters by the mode each task was sent in, one chip
        per task mode in the @{PromptModesScope}'s order, "Code", "Chain",
        "Spec", and "Freeform", each tinted its mode's colour while on, its
        border in that colour and its background a faint tint of it. The
        second group's chips take the theme's accent the same way while on.
        The second filters by where a task stands with the other mode, as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says, with "Can send to Spec" for tasks that
        offer Send to Spec, "Can send to Code" for those that offer Send to
        Code, "Sent" for those already sent to the other mode or being sent
        there, and "Marked done" for those marked done by hand.

        With no chip on, which is how the list starts, every previous task
        shows. Within a group, the chips on combine as either, so a task
        shows when it matches any of them, and the two groups combine as
        both, so with chips on in each, a task shows only when it matches one
        in each. Clicking a chip turns it on or off, and a "Clear" button at
        the bar's right end, shown only while any chip is on, turns them all
        off. A chip that would show no tasks is still shown, its count 0, and
        can still be turned on.

        Filtering only hides tasks from the list; it changes nothing about
        them. A chain whose steps are hidden in part keeps its parent row
        above the steps still shown, and is hidden with its parent only when
        none of its steps shows. Session dividers show only above a session
        with a task shown. The row's count still counts every previous task,
        and while any chip is on, what the row reads, the count, or "Back to
        the latest task" while the list is expanded, is followed by " · N
        shown", N counting the previous tasks the filters show. A hidden task
        stays selected if it was, and is still counted in "N selected" and
        sent by the batch actions; an open task that is filtered out closes.
        With every task filtered out, the list reads "No previous tasks match
        these filters", muted, centred. The filters are kept while the list is
        closed and opened again, and each open project keeps its own, as the
        @{OpenProjectsScope} says, but they are not saved with the project.
        Previous answers have no filter bar.

    chainedTasks:
        A prompt sent in Chain runs as steps, each saved in the history as a
        task of its own: first the Chain task itself, which writes the spec;
        then the same prompt sent to Code, told what the spec step did; and,
        when the chain asks for a post-build spec update, the same prompt sent

export ui-component ChatInputScope:
    concept: {ChatInputConcept}

concept ChatInputConcept:
    pitch:
        A multi-line, syntax-highlighted textbox that accepts plain text as well
        as snippets of Piton.

    shape: {ChatInputShape}

shape ChatInputShape:
    description:
        Input on the left, send button on the right.

        The body beneath the tabs has 8 pixels of padding, on the same flat
        surface as the selected tab, the ribbon's tab row colour, #333333 in
        dark mode, untinted by the mode, and joined to the selected tab with
        no line between them. In it, the text input sits in a dark box on the
        theme's darkest surface, #111111 in dark mode, with corners rounded 4
        pixels and no border, as tall as the column
        of buttons beside it, 8 pixels from it, and taller when its text
        needs more. The text sits 8 pixels in from the box's top, left, and
        right, and grows down through the box. Clicking anywhere in the box
        beneath the text puts focus in the text, except while a preview
        shows. The preview shows in the same box, its content inset 8 pixels
        all round.

        At the right, a column of three buttons, 88 pixels wide, 8 pixels
        apart, each as tall as the input's single row: Send at the top, then
        Queue, then Preview, each the column's full width, flat, with no
        border or shadow and corners rounded 2 pixels. Send has a paper-plane
        send icon before its label, in semibold text, and keeps its split
        chevron, the send menu staying the only way to reach "Send to task".
        Queue and Preview are flat buttons on the theme's base surface,
        #444444 in dark mode, their labels in the theme's text colour, a step
        lighter on hover, doing what the
        send menu's options of those names do, with tooltips saying that
        Queue queues the prompt even while the harness is free, and that
        Preview previews the compiled prompt. They are offered just as the
        menu is: both are disabled while the input is empty, while a preview
        shows, and while a queued prompt is edited, and Queue is also
        disabled on the Ask tab, since a question never queues.

        <Enter> allows for creating new lines, like Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it to
        the ${HarnessIntegrationScope}

        Sending sends the prompt in the selected tab's mode, as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says. While the harness is working, the send
        button on the Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform tabs reads "Queue", since the prompt
        will queue. On the Ask tab it always reads "Send", because a question is
        never queued. The button is only disabled while the input is empty.

    instructions:
        - @{ChatInputInstruction}

    sendOptions:
        splitButton:
            The send button is a split button: the send or queue button itself,
            and joined to its right, a narrow half with a chevron that opens a
            menu of other ways to send the prompt, above the button, its right
            edge lined up with the button's. The chevron half is disabled
            whenever the send half is, and while a preview shows, and its
            tooltip says it shows more ways to send, with its shortcut.

        keyboard:
            <Ctrl+Shift+Enter> (<Cmd+Shift+Enter> on macOS) in the chat input
            opens the menu with its first option highlighted, and does nothing
            while the input is empty or a preview shows. While it is open, the
            text keeps focus, <Up> and <Down> move the highlight, wrapping
            around, <Enter> picks the highlighted option, and <Escape> closes
            the menu, as does pressing <Ctrl+Shift+Enter> again or the mouse
            anywhere outside it. Each option highlights on hover, and clicking
            one picks it.

        options:
            The menu's options, in order:
            - "Preview Compiled Prompt", with an eye icon
            - "Queue", with a list icon, which queues the prompt rather than sending it, even while the harness is free, as the queue of the @{PromptEditor} says; like the send button, it clears the input. On the Ask tab it is disabled, since a question never queues, and the highlight passes over it
            - "Send to task", with a send icon, only while a task is running with a harness that can be fed more, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, and its output is shown, the previous tasks not expanded over it; never on the Ask tab, where a question runs on its own. It sends what is typed, and what is attached, to the running task instead of queueing it, as the @{PromptSendingScope} says, and clears the input as sending does. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS) still queues, as the send button does

    editingQueued:
        Editing a queued prompt, from the queue of the @{PromptEditor}, sets
        aside the prompt being written, its attachments, and the selected tab,
        and puts the queued prompt's text in the input, its attachments above
        it, and its mode's tab selected, with the cursor at the end of the text.
        Above the attachments, a row with a pencil icon reads
        "Editing queued prompt N", its place in the queue, and at its right,
        muted, "Ctrl+Enter to save · Esc to cancel" (with ⌘ on macOS). The send
        button reads "Save", its tooltip saying it saves the queued prompt, and
        the send menu isn't offered.

        Everything in the input works as ever while editing, tabs included.
        <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS), or Save, saves the edit, in the tab
        selected then, and <Escape>, when nothing else in the input takes it,
        cancels it. Either way, the prompt that was set aside comes back just as
        it was. Saving an empty prompt isn't possible, just as sending one
        isn't. Editing another queued prompt meanwhile first cancels the edit in
        progress; so does switching projects.

    preview:
        Preview Compiled Prompt compiles the prompt as it would be sent from the
        selected tab, its hidden anchor, attachments, and mode's system prompt
        included, without sending it, saving it to the history, or building the
        spec first. In place of the text input, the chat input then shows what
        the harness would receive: the compiled prompt, as a sent task's
        compiled prompt is shown, beneath a row reading "Compiled prompt" with,
        at its right, muted, "Ctrl+Enter to send · Esc to edit" (with ⌘ on
        macOS). While it compiles, the row shows a spinner and "Compiling…"; a
        prompt that fails to compile shows why, in the theme's error colour, in
        place of the compiled prompt. The preview grows with what it shows, up
        to 40% of the window's height, and scrolls beyond that. The tabs,
        attachments, and send button stay as they are.

        The preview has keyboard focus. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS), or
        the send button, sends the prompt just as sending from the text input
        would, and the chat input goes back to an empty text input. <Escape>
        goes back to the text input with the prompt and attachments as they
        were, the cursor where it was. Switching tabs while previewing goes back
        to the text input too, since the prompt would compile differently.

    tabs:
        The tabs along the top of the chat input, one for each mode.

        overview:
            The input and buttons live inside the body of a tab bar, a flat
            strip 32 pixels tall on the ribbon's command area colour, #222222
            in dark mode, with no line anywhere in it, whether beneath it,
            between its tabs, or around them. Each tab is only its label, in
            small text, with 8 pixels to each side of it and no border, and
            its label is always in its mode's colour at full strength, of the
            @{PromptModesScope}, whether selected or not: Code red, Spec blue,
            Ask green, and Freeform grey. The selected tab is marked only by
            its background, the same surface as the body beneath it, so it
            reads as a tab joined to that body; unselected tabs have none, and
            show the strip, lightening a little on hover. There is a tab for each of the
            @{PromptModesScope}, in their order: Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, and
            Freeform. Code, Spec, Ask, and Freeform are ordinary tabs. Chain is also a tab, just a
            small one, because it only shows an icon. All five sit flush against
            each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has more padding than a
            normal tab.

            The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so
            Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before
            switching tabs changes the code and the spec together.

            Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to
            Chain to Spec to Ask to Freeform and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other
            way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too,
            not <Cmd>.

            <Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text
            either. They move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next
            or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the
            completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.

        chain:
            Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than
            a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it
            selects both Code and Spec. It never shows a focus outline, and its
            icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two
            is selected.

            Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits
            between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of
            them.

            Chain, like every tab, has no line along its bottom or sides, in
            combined mode or separate, since the tab bar draws no lines at all.
            Nothing draws a line beneath Chain and then hides it, since a
            hidden line can show again wherever rounding to the display's
            pixels uncovers it.

            Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it
            animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both
            its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they
            meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both.
            Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected,
            Code and Spec both show as selected, one continuous background
            beneath the two of them and Chain, reading as a single unified
            tab. Chain itself has a transparent background, so the joined Code
            and Spec show through underneath it.

        help:
            To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of
            help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as
            another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted
            text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet
            note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather
            than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.

            It reads what the selected tab's mode is for, as the
            @{PromptModesScope} says.

        session:
            At the far right of the bar, at the right end of the help text,
            sits how much context the selected tab's conversation holds, then a
            New conversation button. The questions of the Ask tab have a
            conversation of their own, and the other tabs share the tasks', as
            the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, so the figure is the Ask tab's
            conversation while it is selected, and the tasks' on any other tab.

            The figure reads "Context", then the number of tokens, short and
            extra small, muted: "850", "42.1k", "123k", or "1.2M", to a decimal
            place below a hundred of a unit. It follows each reply as the
            harness reports it. While the next prompt would start a new
            conversation, as when the project has none yet or New conversation
            was just pressed, it reads "Context 0". Its tooltip says how many
            tokens the conversation the next prompt carries on holds, or that
            the next prompt starts a new conversation.

            New conversation is a small ghost button with a sparkles icon,
            reading "New conversation". Pressing it starts a new conversation
            for the selected tab: the tasks' on Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform, the
            questions' on Ask. The next run in that tab, or in any tab sharing
            its conversation, starts a new one with no context instead of
            carrying on, and the figure reads "Context 0". A run of the
            conversation left that is still going finishes as it would, but
            neither it nor the project's history brings that conversation back,
            even once the project is closed and opened again, as the
            @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says.

            It can be pressed while a run in that conversation is under way, a
            task on Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform, or any question on Ask, without
            waiting for it to finish. Pressed while a task runs, the prompts
            sent meanwhile queue as ever, and the next task to run from the
            queue, the first in it, starts a new conversation with no context,
            the ones after it carrying that one on. That holds even when the
            running task is the first of its conversation and the harness
            hasn't yet said which conversation it is: once it does, it isn't
            carried on either.

            Whether a task starts a new conversation is part of its prompt,
            recorded in its hidden anchor. Pressed for the tasks with prompts
            queued, New conversation marks the first in the queue, saving it
            again with the project, so it still starts the new conversation
            once the project is closed and opened again. With nothing queued,
            the next task sent or queued takes the mark. Cancelling the marked
            prompt passes the mark on to the one that now comes first, or,
            with nothing left queued, to the next task sent or queued. A task
            marked this way never carries on the conversation before it when it
            runs.

            <Ctrl+N> while in the chat input does just what pressing New
            conversation does, for the selected tab, and nothing while the
            button is disabled. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.

            Its tooltip says which conversation it resets, with its shortcut:
            "Start a new conversation for tasks (Ctrl+N)" or
            "Start a new conversation for questions (Ctrl+N)", adding, while a run in
            it is under way, that the run finishes in the conversation left.
            It is disabled only while that conversation has nothing to carry
            on and no run in it is under way, its tooltip then saying the next
            task, or question, already starts a new conversation.

            Both sit on the bar's bottom line, which runs beneath them as it does
            beneath the help text, and neither is cut off: the help text gives
            way to them when the bar is narrow.

        usage:
            Just right of the context figure, before New conversation, sits the
            agent's usage: how much of the harness picked, of the
            @{HarnessIntegrationScope}, has been used, as Claude Code's /usage
            shows it. Its summary is short and extra small, muted like the
            context figure: "Usage", then the share used of the plan limit
            nearest to running out, such as "Usage 42%", turning the theme's
            warning colour from 80% and its error colour once the limit is
            reached. When the harness reports no plan limits, the summary is
            the cost of this project's runs since it was opened, such as
            "Usage $1.24", or the tokens they used, as the context figure is
            written, when it reports no cost either. Until anything has been
            reported, it reads "Usage", with nothing after it.

            Clicking the summary opens a popover above it with all the details,
            each group headed, and each figure labelled:

            \\
            - Plan limits: each limit the harness reports, such as the current
              session's and the week's, with the share used as a bar and a
              percentage, and when it resets.
            - Conversation: the context the selected tab's conversation holds,
              and its input, output, cache-read, and cache-written tokens, and
              its cost.
            - This project: the same totals for every run in the project since
              it was opened, tasks and questions, and how many runs there were.
            - The harness and model the figures came from, and when they were
              last reported.
            \\

            A group, or a figure, the harness doesn't report is left out rather
            than shown as zero, and when nothing has been reported the popover
            says so. The figures come from what the harness reports as its runs
            go, never from running anything of its own to ask, and update in
            place while the popover is open, following each reply. Clicking
            outside the popover, or pressing Escape, closes it. The summary's
            tooltip says to click for the details. Like the context figure, it
            is never cut off: the help text gives way to it.

        slice:
            Just left of the context figure sits the Slice toggle: a small ghost
            button with a scissors icon, reading "Slice", which shows as
            selected while it is on. It starts off. Its tooltip says what the
            prompt is sent as: while off, the prompt written as a spec, its
            references linking to the spec they name; while on, the prompt with
            the `piton slice` of each spec it references. Clicking it turns it
            on or off, and it applies to every tab, Ask included. It stays as it
            is across sends, tab switches, and project switches, as the prompt
            being written does, and the help text gives way to it as it does to
            the session controls.

        colour:
            The selected tab and the tab body holding the input are not tinted:
            they stay the flat surface the description gives, whatever the
            mode, the mode showing in the tab labels' colours and the send
            button's. The send button's colour transitions smoothly whenever
            the selected tab changes, straight from the old tab's colour to the
            new one's. The tabs wrap around, so pressing
            <Ctrl+Tab> on Freeform fades grey straight to Code's red, and
            <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Freeform's grey;
            neither lights up Chain, Spec, or Ask on the way. A fade to or from
            Freeform's grey keeps the other tab's hue, only draining or filling
            its colour, so it never passes through another hue. Between Code
            and Spec it passes through Chain's colour, whatever colours they
            have been given in the theme editor.

            The send button, both its halves, is a muted slate: the selected
            mode's colour, purple with Chain selected, mixed well down into the
            theme's base surface, so it reads as a quiet hint of the mode,
            about #3b4252 for Spec's blue in dark mode, standing apart from
            Queue and Preview without shouting.
            Its label and chevron are in the theme's text colour for a solid
            hue, and the line between its halves is only faintly darker or
            lighter than it, half as far as its hover, just enough to part
            them. Disabled, the button fades as a disabled button does, in the
            same colour, and the line fades with the half it borders, never
            staying solid across a faded button.

    systemPrompt:
        The selected tab is the mode a prompt is sent in, and each mode's system
        prompt is sent with it, as the @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says.

    ask:
        Ask is for simply asking a question, which runs as the
        @{PromptModesScope} says. Any number of questions can be asked, and they
        all run at the same time; asking another never stops or waits for one
        already running.

        Each question's progress and results are shown in a @{TaskTableScope}.
        The questions stack directly above the tabs, the newest nearest them, in
        a column that pushes the message list up to make room rather than
        covering it, so none of a running task's progress is ever hidden behind
        them. Each slides up out of the chat input with an animation as it is
        asked, the message list giving way above it. While the harness works on
        a question, it is a single row showing the latest thing the harness did.
        A finished question is a row with its status and first line.

        However many questions are asked, the stack is only as tall as its
        rows, up to 240 pixels, the queue's most, and scrolls beyond that with
        a @{ScrollbarScope}, kept on the newest question, nearest the tabs, as
        each is asked. Once it holds more than fit, the stack lays out only
        the rows in view, as a table does, so a long stack costs no more to show, scroll, or animate than a
        short one, and the drawer's bottom follows the stack's top as ever.

        Once a question is complete, it opens onto a heading, with its status
        and first line, above its full task table, in the @{AnswerDrawerScope},
        which it fills, the table scrolling once it is taller, with its lock to
        the bottom off to start with. Only one question is open at a time:
        opening another closes the one open back down to its row. An open
        question leaves the stack for the drawer. Clicking an open question's
        heading closes it down to its row in the stack, and clicking a finished
        question's row opens it again. Each question has a close button, which
        removes it and stops it if it is still running, leaving the others
        running. A closed question becomes a previous answer.

    answerSteps:
        For a question, only the answer matters, so wherever a finished
        question's task table is shown, an open question and a previous answer,
        the table collapses the steps leading up to the answer, as the
        @{TaskTableScope} says. A question closed into the previous answers
        starts collapsed again. Tasks are never collapsed like this: see the
        @{MessageList}.

    previousAnswers:
        Previous answers are a @{HistoryListScope}, shown only while the Ask tab
        is selected, at the top of the questions stacked above the tabs. It
        lists every question asked before and closed: those saved with the
        project and those closed since. Its row reads "No previous answers",
        "1 previous answer", or "N previous answers", and while expanded,
        "Back to the questions". Each previous answer offers Resend, which asks
        its question again, as the @{PromptSendingScope} says. Expanded, the
        row and the list go into the @{AnswerDrawerScope}, sliding up from on
        top of any question rows still in the stack. The questions asked from
        now on carry on the conversation the latest of them left off.

    answerDrawer: @{AnswerDrawerScope}

    selectingAnswerText:
        The text of an answer being viewed, in the answer drawer, whether an
        open question or a previous answer, can be selected by dragging across
        it, as any text can. A drag that selects text ending within the drawer
        shows a @{SelectionPopoverScope} with two buttons: "Copy", with a copy
        icon, and "Attach to prompt", with a paperclip icon.

        Copy puts the selected text on the clipboard. Attach to prompt adds it
        to the prompt as an attachment. Either one clears the selection. The
        popover also closes when the drawer closes.

    attachments:
        What is attached to the prompt is listed above the text input, between
        the tabs and the input, one row per attachment in the order they were
        attached, and only while there is anything attached. An attached piece
        of text shows a quote icon, the text's first line cut off with an
        ellipsis, and, when it runs to more than one line, how many lines it
        has, muted, and at the right end a small button with a cross, whose
        tooltip says it removes the attachment, which removes just that one.

        Images can be attached too: pasted from the clipboard while the chat
        input has focus, dropped onto the chat input from the file manager, or
        chosen with a small ghost button with an image icon, whose tooltip says
        "Attach images", on the tab row between the last tab and the help
        text, which opens the platform's file picker for any files, several at
        once, since the picker can't be limited to images. Pasting an image
        attaches it rather than putting anything in the text, even when the
        clipboard holds text as well; every image on the clipboard is
        attached, and a clipboard with no image pastes its text as usual.
        Several files dropped or chosen at once are attached in their order,
        each on its own merits. An image is known by its content, not
        its name, and only PNG, JPEG, GIF, and WebP are taken: anything else
        pasted, dropped, or chosen, BMP, TIFF, and SVG included, is not
        attached, and a warning notification titled "Not attached" says it
        isn't an image. An image larger than 5 MB is not attached either, and
        the same notification says it is too large. A folder dropped or chosen
        isn't an image either, and a file that can't be read is not attached,
        the same notification saying it couldn't be read, and why. Each file
        left out has its own notification, and the others are still attached.

        Files can be dropped only on the chat input itself, its tabs, the
        attachments, and the text input; dropping them on the message list
        above it does nothing. While files are dragged over the chat input,
        its background is highlighted with the accent's fill, laid about a
        quarter of the way over it.

        An attached
        image's row shows a small thumbnail, its file name, or "Pasted image"
        for one pasted, and its size in pixels, muted, with the same remove
        button; hovering the thumbnail shows the image larger, at most 320
        pixels. Images and text are listed together in the order they were
        attached while the prompt is written. A prompt taken back into the
        input, as when a queued prompt is edited, lists its text first, then
        its images, each image named by its saved file, a pasted one
        included.

        Attachments belong to the prompt being written, not to a tab: switching
        tabs keeps them all, and they go with the prompt whichever tab it is
        sent from. When the prompt is sent, its attachments are sent along with
        it and the list empties, as the text input does. A queued prompt keeps
        the attachments it was sent with.

    projects:
        The questions stacked above the tabs, the open answer, and the previous
        answers belong to their project, as the @{OpenProjectsScope} says:
        switching projects shows those of the project switched to, while the
        questions of other projects carry on running in the background. The
        prompt being written, its attachments, the selected tab, and the Slice
        toggle stay as they are across a switch, and are sent to the project on screen.

    escape:
        Pressing <Escape> while in the chat input takes focus out of the chat
        input. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS) brings it back, from
        anywhere the chat input isn't beneath something else, as the
        @{MainWindowScope} says.

    growToFit:
        The text input is a @{GrowingTextInputScope} growing to 12 rows at most.

To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of
            help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as
            another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted
            text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet
            note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather
            than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.

            It reads what the selected tab's mode is for, as the
            @{PromptModesScope} says.

        session:
            At the far right of the bar, at the right end of the help text,
            sits how much context the selected tab's conversation holds, then a
            New conversation button. The questions of the Ask tab have a
            conversation of their own, and the other tabs share the tasks', as
            the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, so the figure is the Ask tab's
            conversation while it is selected, and the tasks' on any other tab.

            The figure reads "Context", then the number of tokens, short and
            extra small, muted: "850", "42.1k", "123k", or "1.2M", to a decimal
            place below a hundred of a unit. It follows each reply as the
            harness reports it. While the next prompt would start a new
            conversation, as when the project has none yet or New conversation
            was just pressed, it reads "Context 0". Its tooltip says how many
            tokens the conversation the next prompt carries on holds, or that
            the next prompt starts a new conversation.

            New conversation is a small ghost button with a sparkles icon,
            reading "New conversation". Pressing it starts a new conversation
            for the selected tab: the tasks' on Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform, the
            questions' on Ask. The next run in that tab, or in any tab sharing
            its conversation, starts a new one with no context instead of
            carrying on, and the figure reads "Context 0". A run of the
            conversation left that is still going finishes as it would, but
            neither it nor the project's history brings that conversation back,
            even once the project is closed and opened again, as the
            @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says.

            It can be pressed while a run in that conversation is under way, a
            task on Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform, or any question on Ask, without
            waiting for it to finish. Pressed while a task runs, the prompts
            sent meanwhile queue as ever, and the next task to run from the
            queue, the first in it, starts a new conversation with no context,
            the ones after it carrying that one on. That holds even when the
            running task is the first of its conversation and the harness
            hasn't yet said which conversation it is: once it does, it isn't
            carried on either.

            Whether a task starts a new conversation is part of its prompt,
            recorded in its hidden anchor. Pressed for the tasks with prompts
            queued, New conversation marks the first in the queue, saving it
            again with the project, so it still starts the new conversation
            once the project is closed and opened again. With nothing queued,
            the next task sent or queued takes the mark. Cancelling the marked
            prompt passes the mark on to the one that now comes first, or,
            with nothing left queued, to the next task sent or queued. A task
            marked this way never carries on the conversation before it when it
            runs.

            <Ctrl+N> while in the chat input does just what pressing New
            conversation does, for the selected tab, and nothing while the
            button is disabled. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.

            Its tooltip says which conversation it resets, with its shortcut:
            "Start a new conversation for tasks (Ctrl+N)" or
            "Start a new conversation for questions (Ctrl+N)", adding, while a run in
            it is under way, that the run finishes in the conversation left.
            It is disabled only while that conversation has nothing to carry
            on and no run in it is under way, its tooltip then saying the next
            task, or question, already starts a new conversation.

            Both sit on the bar's bottom line, which runs beneath them as it does
            beneath the help text, and neither is cut off: the help text gives
            way to them when the bar is narrow.

        usage:
            same colour, and the line fades with the half it borders, never
            staying solid across a faded button.

    systemPrompt:
        The selected tab is the mode a prompt is sent in, and each mode's system
        prompt is sent with it, as the @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says.

    ask:
        Ask is for simply asking a question, which runs as the
        @{PromptModesScope} says. Any number of questions can be asked, and they
        all run at the same time; asking another never stops or waits for one
        already running.

        Each question's progress and results are shown in a @{TaskTableScope}.
        The questions stack directly above the tabs, the newest nearest them, in
        a column that pushes the message list up to make room rather than
        covering it, so none of a running task's progress is ever hidden behind
        them. Each slides up out of the chat input with an animation as it is
        asked, the message list giving way above it. While the harness works on
        a question, it is a single row showing the latest thing the harness did.
        A finished question is a row with its status and first line.

        However many questions are asked, the stack is only as tall as its
        rows, up to 240 pixels, the queue's most, and scrolls beyond that with
        a @{ScrollbarScope}, kept on the newest question, nearest the tabs, as
        each is asked. Once it holds more than fit, the stack lays out only
        the rows in view, as a table does, so a long stack costs no more to show, scroll, or animate than a
        short one, and the drawer's bottom follows the stack's top as ever.

        Once a question is complete, it opens onto a heading, with its status
        and first line, above its full task table, in the @{AnswerDrawerScope},
        which it fills, the table scrolling once it is taller, with its lock to
        the bottom off to start with. Only one question is open at a time:
        opening another closes the one open back down to its row. An open
        question leaves the stack for the drawer. Clicking an open question's
        heading closes it down to its row in the stack, and clicking a finished
        question's row opens it again. Each question has a close button, which
        removes it and stops it if it is still running, leaving the others
        running. A closed question becomes a previous answer.

    answerSteps:
        For a question, only the answer matters, so wherever a finished
        question's task table is shown, an open question and a previous answer,
        the table collapses the steps leading up to the answer, as the
        @{TaskTableScope} says. A question closed into the previous answers
        starts collapsed again. Tasks are never collapsed like this: see the
        @{MessageList}.

    previousAnswers:
        Previous answers are a @{HistoryListScope}, shown only while the Ask tab
        is selected, at the top of the questions stacked above the tabs. It
        lists every question asked before and closed: those saved with the
        project and those closed since. Its row reads "No previous answers",
        "1 previous answer", or "N previous answers", and while expanded,
        "Back to the questions". Each previous answer offers Resend, which asks
        its question again, as the @{PromptSendingScope} says. Expanded, the
        row and the list go into the @{AnswerDrawerScope}, sliding up from on
        top of any question rows still in the stack. The questions asked from
        now on carry on the conversation the latest of them left off.

    answerDrawer: @{AnswerDrawerScope}

    selectingAnswerText:
        The text of an answer being viewed, in the answer drawer, whether an
        open question or a previous answer, can be selected by dragging across
        it, as any text can. A drag that selects text ending within the drawer
        shows a @{SelectionPopoverScope} with two buttons: "Copy", with a copy
        icon, and "Attach to prompt", with a paperclip icon.

        Copy puts the selected text on the clipboard. Attach to prompt adds it
        to the prompt as an attachment. Either one clears the selection. The
        popover also closes when the drawer closes.

    attachments:
        What is attached to the prompt is listed above the text input, between
        the tabs and the input, one row per attachment in the order they were
        attached, and only while there is anything attached. An attached piece
        of text shows a quote icon, the text's first line cut off with an
        ellipsis, and, when it runs to more than one line, how many lines it
        has, muted, and at the right end a small button with a cross, whose
        tooltip says it removes the attachment, which removes just that one.

        Images can be attached too: pasted from the clipboard while the chat
        input has focus, dropped onto the chat input from the file manager, or
        chosen with a small ghost button with an image icon, whose tooltip says
        "Attach images", on the tab row between the last tab and the help
        text, which opens the platform's file picker for any files, several at
        once, since the picker can't be limited to images. Pasting an image
        attaches it rather than putting anything in the text, even when the
        clipboard holds text as well; every image on the clipboard is
        attached, and a clipboard with no image pastes its text as usual.
        Several files dropped or chosen at once are attached in their order,
        each on its own merits. An image is known by its content, not
        its name, and only PNG, JPEG, GIF, and WebP are taken: anything else
        pasted, dropped, or chosen, BMP, TIFF, and SVG included, is not
        attached, and a warning notification titled "Not attached" says it
        isn't an image. An image larger than 5 MB is not attached either, and
        the same notification says it is too large. A folder dropped or chosen
        isn't an image either, and a file that can't be read is not attached,
        the same notification saying it couldn't be read, and why. Each file
        left out has its own notification, and the others are still attached.

        Files can be dropped only on the chat input itself, its tabs, the
        attachments, and the text input; dropping them on the message list
        above it does nothing. While files are dragged over the chat input,
        its background is highlighted with the accent's fill, laid about a
        quarter of the way over it.

        An attached
        image's row shows a small thumbnail, its file name, or "Pasted image"
        for one pasted, and its size in pixels, muted, with the same remove
        button; hovering the thumbnail shows the image larger, at most 320
        pixels. Images and text are listed together in the order they were
        attached while the prompt is written. A prompt taken back into the
        input, as when a queued prompt is edited, lists its text first, then
        its images, each image named by its saved file, a pasted one
        included.

        Attachments belong to the prompt being written, not to a tab: switching
        tabs keeps them all, and they go with the prompt whichever tab it is
        sent from. When the prompt is sent, its attachments are sent along with
        it and the list empties, as the text input does. A queued prompt keeps
        the attachments it was sent with.

    projects:
        The questions stacked above the tabs, the open answer, and the previous
        answers belong to their project, as the @{OpenProjectsScope} says:
        switching projects shows those of the project switched to, while the
        questions of other projects carry on running in the background. The
        prompt being written, its attachments, the selected tab, and the Slice
        toggle stay as they are across a switch, and are sent to the project on screen.

    escape:
        Pressing <Escape> while in the chat input takes focus out of the chat
        input. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS) brings it back, from
        anywhere the chat input isn't beneath something else, as the
        @{MainWindowScope} says.

    growToFit:
        The text input is a @{GrowingTextInputScope} growing to 12 rows at most.
        Its first row lines up with the send button, both at the top of the
        input row, and it grows downward from there.

    autoFocus:
        The chat input should be auto-focused.
